messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 55
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 64

Joseph is a 55-year-old married man who works as a bomb disposal technician for a national security agency. His wife, Nkechi, is the one who gently pushed him to come to therapy—she told him she couldn't watch him drown anymore. In the first few sessions, Joseph sits stiffly, his eyes scanning the room before he speaks. He holds his hands clasped tightly, knuckles white, as if bracing for a shock.

He begins by telling me about the earthquake. It happened three years ago, during what should have been a routine assignment. Joseph was called to a crowded market in a coastal city to dispose of a suspicious device. The device turned out to be a hoax, but just as he was packing up his gear, the ground lurched. He remembers a low, grinding roar that seemed to come from everywhere at once. Buildings swayed, then toppled. The market stalls collapsed like dominoes. Joseph was thrown under a concrete slab, pinned by the rubble. He could hear screaming—people buried beside him, calling for help. He tried to reach a woman whose hand was sticking out of the debris, but the slab was too heavy. The screams stopped after a few minutes. It took rescue workers six hours to dig him out.

Since that day, Joseph has not been the same. He describes a constant, choking dread that sits in his chest, as if the earth is about to shake again. At work, he finds it impossible to concentrate. When he handles a detonator, his hands tremble, and he sees the market instead of the device. Twice he has had to step away from a live ordnance, overcome by a sudden panic that feels exactly like the earthquake—the same roar in his ears, the same crushing weight on his chest. His supervisors have noticed. They moved him to administrative duties, but he still feels the pressure. He avoids the bomb disposal van now, because the smell of diesel and concrete triggers flashbacks.

At home, Joseph has become withdrawn. He no longer joins Nkechi for their evening walks. He stopped gardening, once his solace. The sound of a distant truck backfiring makes him dive for cover, heart hammering. He has nightmares almost every night—always the same: he is buried alive, the woman’s hand reaching for him, but when he wakes, he cannot remember her face. Nkechi says he cries out in his sleep, words she cannot understand. He has not slept beside her in months.

Joseph feels a raw, festering guilt. He replays the moment he could not free that woman. He tells me he should have tried harder, should have ignored the pain in his own leg. He has stopped going to the mosque, because the imam’s sermons about fate and patience feel like an accusation. He says he no longer believes in a merciful God. Instead, he is hollow, irritable. Small things—a dropped cup, a slow driver—send him into a rage that frightens even him.

Therapy is difficult for Joseph. He does not like talking about the earthquake. He shifts in his seat when I ask about the sensations. He prefers to talk about his work, about the mechanical precision of disarming a bomb. But then he stops, and his eyes grow distant. “The last thing I heard,” he says quietly, “was the sound of a child crying.” He does not finish the sentence. He looks at the clock. He is checking the exits.
